topics.title: What Redis Is
topics.description: Redis fundamentals and where its key-oriented, in-memory model fits in an application architecture.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis is a key-oriented server whose strength comes from keeping a working dataset in memory and exposing data structures designed for direct operations. Think in terms of access patterns first: cache a complete value, count events, test membership, maintain order, or rank entities. Redis can be the authoritative store for some workloads, but many applications use it beside a durable database for derived or latency-sensitive state.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Redis is best understood as a high-speed, key-oriented data system in which the application chooses a data structure that matches the operations it performs. Its in-memory working set makes short, direct operations very fast, while persistence and replication can be added when the workload needs recovery or redundancy. The important design idea is not simply “keep data in RAM”; it is to shape the stored representation around the application's questions. A counter, membership test, recent-event feed, ranking, and mutable object each have different access patterns, so they can use different Redis structures. Redis therefore often complements a primary database instead of replacing it. Durable business records, complex relationships, and arbitrary analytical queries may belong elsewhere, while Redis can handle caches, counters, temporary state, queues, rankings, and fast lookups. Good Redis design starts by listing the reads and writes the application must perform, then selecting structures and keys that make those operations direct.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A course platform can keep the authoritative course catalog in a database while using Redis for `cache:course:42`, a string counter such as `views:course:42`, a set such as `course:42:learners`, and a sorted set for popular courses. Each structure exists because it answers a different question efficiently.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use Redis when low-latency access and simple, predictable operations are more important than arbitrary querying. Treat it as one component of the architecture and explicitly decide which data is authoritative, which data is derived, and which data may safely expire.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Imagine Redis as a programmable data-structure server sitting on a very fast memory path. The key is the address; the value is not always one blob. The chosen structure encodes what the application needs to ask quickly.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: An interview answer should distinguish Redis from a simple key-value map: Redis has multiple native structures, atomic commands, expiration, persistence, replication, scripting, and clustering capabilities. Also explain why a database-plus-Redis architecture may be preferable when the system needs durable relational queries or complex transactions. Typical interview questions: Why Redis? When should Redis not be the primary database? Why do data structures matter? What makes Redis fast? What is the difference between cache, database, and coordination use cases?

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not describe Redis as 'just an in-memory cache.' Do not assume persistence makes it equivalent to a relational database. Do not ignore memory overhead, eviction, replication lag, failure recovery, or the consistency of derived data.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Choose Redis when the workload benefits from predictable low-latency operations, high throughput, ephemeral state, counters, rankings, or fast coordination. Be cautious when the workload needs complex ad-hoc queries, large analytical scans, or durable relational constraints.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: For a shopping platform, keep authoritative orders in a durable database while Redis holds sessions, hot product responses, counters, rankings, and short-lived workflow state. Each key family has an explicit owner and recovery policy.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related ideas include strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, Streams, TTL, eviction policies, persistence, replication, Sentinel, Cluster, transactions, Lua, ACLs, and cache-aside design.

topics.title: Getting Started
topics.description: Redis server, client interaction, basic commands, server inspection, and logical databases.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Getting started means learning the Redis request/response model, connecting a client, issuing commands, inspecting state, and understanding the selected logical database. The goal is to form a state-based mental model: every command changes or observes server state.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A Redis deployment has a server process that owns the data and clients that communicate with it using commands. A beginner should first learn the request/response cycle rather than memorizing a long command list: connect, write a value, read it, inspect server information, and understand the logical database context. The classic command-line workflow uses `redis-cli`, while the server listens on the default port discussed by the supplied material, 6379. Logical database numbers provide separate key namespaces within one instance, but they are not equivalent to separate machines or independent Redis deployments. For learning, start with tiny experiments and observe the result of every command. This builds an accurate mental model for later topics such as TTL, transactions, scanning, and persistence.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Start with `SET greeting \"hello\"` and then `GET greeting`. Next inspect server information with `INFO`, and, where logical databases are enabled in the deployment, switch context with `SELECT 1` and verify that a key created there is separate from the same key name in database 0.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use a disposable development instance for experiments. Keep a small command transcript while learning so that you can connect each command to the resulting state rather than treating Redis as a black box.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Treat the CLI as a laboratory. Write one command, predict the response, run it, and then inspect the resulting state. This habit makes later concepts such as transactions and expiration much easier.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Use a local development server and redis-cli for first experiments. Learn command syntax, return types, key existence, type inspection, TTL inspection, and safe deletion before moving to advanced administration.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not expose a development Redis instance to the public internet. Do not assume SELECT creates an independent server. Do not use destructive commands casually against shared environments.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interviewers often ask what redis-cli is, what port Redis commonly uses, how to inspect a key's type, and whether logical databases provide true isolation. Explain that logical databases are namespaces inside one Redis server, not separate failure or security boundaries.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A developer reproduces a cache bug locally by setting a key, checking its type and TTL, changing the value, and inspecting INFO output. The same workflow later becomes part of operational troubleshooting.

sections.content: Connect this topic to redis-cli, RESP, commands and replies, SELECT, TYPE, TTL, INFO, CONFIG, authentication, and client libraries.

topics.title: Keys and Values
topics.description: Key naming, value representation, namespaces, and the access-pattern mindset.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Keys and Values is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. Redis features are easiest to use well when the access pattern, lifecycle, consistency requirement, and failure behavior are explicit.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A Redis key is the address through which an application reaches a stored value. Redis does not interpret a colon as a namespace operator, but names such as `user:42`, `cart:user:42`, and `cache:product:900` create a human-readable convention. Good names are predictable, sufficiently descriptive, and not unnecessarily long because key bytes also consume memory. Values can be scalar text or serialized application data, but Redis generally does not infer the application's object schema from a generic value. This makes the access-pattern rule essential: if an application frequently asks for users by email, storing only `user:<id>` objects is not enough to make email lookup direct. A separate lookup structure can map email to ID. The same principle applies to every alternate query. Instead of expecting Redis to discover relationships by scanning unrelated keys, model those relationships explicitly.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a customer service application, use `customer:804` for the main record and `customer:lookup:email` for an email-to-ID mapping. A login request first resolves the email to `804`, then reads `customer:804`.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Define a key naming convention before a Redis-backed feature grows. Document the owner and lifecycle of each key family, especially whether it is authoritative, derived, temporary, or a lookup index.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Build the mental model around four questions: what state does Redis maintain, what operation does the application need, what work does the server perform, and what happens when the workload becomes large or a node fails? For Keys and Values, a convenient command is not automatically a good production design. The surrounding data model and operational policy determine whether the feature remains predictable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: explain Keys and Values in terms of the problem it solves, the relevant command or data structure, expected complexity or latency behavior, and the main trade-offs. A strong answer also compares it with the closest alternative and gives one production failure mode. Avoid command-only answers; explain why the design is appropriate.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls with Keys and Values include choosing it without defining the access pattern, ignoring collection size or response size, assuming Redis provides stronger consistency or durability than configured, and overlooking retries, expiration, or failure behavior. Test boundary cases explicitly and document the assumptions that make the design safe.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Keys and Values when its native semantics directly match the workload and its operational cost is bounded. Avoid it when the same requirement can be served more simply, when the data must support arbitrary querying that Redis does not model directly, or when the feature's failure semantics do not satisfy the business requirement.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In production, treat Keys and Values as part of an observable design. Define ownership of the keys, expected cardinality, latency target, error/retry behavior, memory impact, monitoring signals, and recovery procedure. Load-test realistic data sizes and include failure scenarios before making the feature a critical dependency.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include Redis key naming, data structures, command complexity, pipelining, transactions, expiration, persistence, replication, observability, and capacity planning. Connect Keys and Values to neighboring Redis features rather than learning it as an isolated command.

topics.title: Memory and Persistence
topics.description: Memory planning plus snapshot and append-oriented persistence trade-offs.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis memory is the active working set, while persistence determines how state can be reconstructed after process or host failure. Capacity planning must include keys, values, data-structure overhead, allocator fragmentation, buffers, replicas, and temporary peaks.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Redis's fast working set depends on memory, so capacity planning must consider much more than the number of keys. Key bytes, value bytes, data-structure overhead, collection cardinality, replicas, client buffers, and temporary work can all contribute to RAM usage. Persistence changes the failure model: a snapshot captures state at a point in time, while an append-oriented approach records changes so state can be reconstructed. The two approaches have different write overhead, recovery characteristics, and amounts of recent data that may be exposed after a failure. Persistence should therefore follow business recovery requirements. Losing a few minutes of a disposable cache may be acceptable; losing committed business state may not be. Persistence also does not remove the need for capacity planning because the live working set still has to fit comfortably in memory.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose a service keeps 2 million session keys averaging 1.5 KB each. The rough payload alone is several gigabytes, before Redis overhead, fragmentation, replicas, and operational headroom. A snapshot may protect a recovery point, but it does not make the live dataset smaller.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Estimate average and worst-case object sizes, measure real memory usage, leave operational headroom, and test restoration. Treat persistence settings as part of the recovery design rather than as a generic performance toggle.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The mental model is two separate questions: 'How much live state can RAM hold safely?' and 'How much state can I recover after failure?' Persistence answers the second; memory sizing answers the first.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Snapshot-oriented persistence creates point-in-time recovery files, while append-oriented persistence records write operations so a dataset can be reconstructed. The durability window, write overhead, recovery time, and operational workflow depend on the chosen configuration.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common mistakes include filling memory to the limit, ignoring replica memory, treating a local persistence file as a disaster-recovery plan, and never testing restoration.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interviewers commonly test RDB versus AOF, whether replication equals backup, and what happens after a crash. A strong answer separates live redundancy from historical recovery and explains RPO/RTO.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A production team uses persistence for restart recovery, copies recovery artifacts to protected off-host storage, monitors memory headroom, and periodically performs restore drills.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include RDB, AOF, fsync policy, rewrite/compaction, replication, backups, eviction, maxmemory, fragmentation, RPO, and RTO.

topics.title: Strings
topics.description: Scalar values, serialized objects, counters, ranges, append operations, and bit-oriented storage.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis strings store one scalar byte sequence and are useful for complete-value access, counters, flags, tokens, cached payloads, and compact serialized data. Numeric commands operate on string representations that contain valid integers or floating-point values.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Strings are the simplest Redis value type and are useful whenever the application can treat a value as one scalar or one serialized unit. Typical uses include flags, tokens, counters, cached API responses, compact serialized objects, and byte-oriented data. A string is especially convenient when the application normally reads or replaces the whole value. If individual fields change independently, repeatedly decoding and rewriting a large serialized object may be less attractive than a hash. Numeric strings can participate in atomic increment operations, making them useful for counters without an application-side read-modify-write race. Strings also support operations such as length, ranges, append, and bit manipulation. The important boundary is representation: a value stored as `\"Maya\"` is not a numeric counter simply because another command can operate on strings that contain numbers.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A news site can store `article:900:views` as a numeric string and increment it as visits arrive. It can separately store `cache:article:900` as a serialized response with a TTL. The two keys have different purposes even though both use the string type.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Choose strings for whole-value access, counters, cache entries, and naturally byte-oriented data. Avoid treating serialized formats as arbitrary strings when field-level mutation or structured querying is a frequent requirement.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The important distinction is logical type versus Redis storage type. A serialized JSON document is still one Redis string; Redis does not automatically expose its JSON fields as native hash fields.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Use whole-value operations when the application normally reads or replaces the entire payload. Use atomic increment commands for counters instead of client-side read-modify-write sequences. Choose hashes when independent fields need frequent mutation.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Pitfalls include storing very large blobs without sizing responses, repeatedly rewriting large serialized objects for tiny field changes, and assuming numeric commands will accept arbitrary string contents.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Know SET/GET, MGET/MSET, INCR/DECR, INCRBY, EXPIRE, SET with expiration options, APPEND, GETRANGE, and bit-oriented commands at a conceptual level. Be ready to explain why a counter is still stored as a string type.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A rate-limiter stores a counter key with an expiration window, while a cache stores a serialized API response under a separate key. Different lifecycles keep the design understandable.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: hashes, TTL, atomic increments, bitmaps, serialization formats, cache-aside, pipelining, and Lua.

topics.title: Hashes
topics.description: Field-value objects, partial updates, lookup maps, and consistency implications of secondary indexes.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Hashes represent field-value pairs under one top-level key. They are natural for mutable objects whose fields are accessed independently, and they can also represent compact lookup maps.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A Redis hash stores multiple field-value pairs under one top-level key, making it a natural representation for objects whose fields are accessed independently. Instead of replacing an entire serialized customer object when only the city changes, an application can update the city field directly. Hashes also work well as compact lookup maps, such as email-to-user-ID mappings, and as grouped collections where the top-level key identifies the owner. The major modeling benefit is locality: related fields can live together while individual fields remain addressable. The major risk appears when a hash is used as a manually maintained index. Whenever an indexed attribute changes, the application must remove the old mapping and create the new one. If that update is missed, reads can follow stale references. Hashes therefore simplify field updates but do not eliminate consistency responsibilities.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Store `employee:301` with fields `name`, `team`, `level`, and `office`. If the employee moves teams, update only `team`. Separately, `employee:lookup:email` can map `arjun@example.test` to `301` without duplicating the employee object.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use hashes for independently updated object fields and simple lookup maps. Define rules for creation, updates, deletion, and index repair so secondary mappings cannot silently drift from the primary object.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of a hash as a small object namespace behind one Redis key. The top-level key identifies the object or map; fields identify individual attributes.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Field-level operations avoid rewriting an entire serialized object when only one attribute changes. However, hashes are not relational tables: there are no automatic secondary indexes or foreign-key constraints, so alternate lookups must be modeled explicitly.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Watch for stale manually maintained indexes, unbounded field counts, and assumptions that all application object behavior should be placed into one hash.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interviewers often ask when to use a hash versus a string. Say hash for independently updated fields; string for whole-value replacement or serialized payloads. Also discuss memory/cardinality considerations for very large hashes.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A user profile is stored as a hash while an email-to-user-ID map is maintained separately. Profile changes update fields directly, and login resolves the alternate identifier through the lookup map.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: HGET/HSET/HINCRBY, field cardinality, secondary indexes, serialization, key naming, and transactions.

topics.title: Lists
topics.description: Ordered collections, recent-item feeds, bounded lists, queues, blocking consumption, and batching.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis lists are ordered sequences. They fit recent-item windows, simple FIFO/LIFO queues, activity histories, and other cases where insertion order is part of the requirement.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Lists represent ordered sequences and are useful when position matters. They fit recent-item feeds, activity histories, and simple producer-consumer queues. A common pattern is to add a new item at one end and retain only a bounded number of entries so the structure cannot grow without limit. For queues, producers add jobs while workers remove them from the opposite side, creating FIFO behavior when the chosen operations are consistent. Blocking list operations can let workers wait for work instead of repeatedly polling an empty queue. Lists often store identifiers rather than full objects; this keeps the list small and lets the application retrieve the current object separately. That design introduces network round trips, so multi-key retrieval and pipelining become important when many IDs must be resolved. A list is therefore strongest when order is central and the required window or queue semantics are clear.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a learning dashboard, keep the latest 25 lesson events in `activity:user:73`. Add new event IDs to the front and trim old entries. When the user opens the dashboard, retrieve the IDs and then fetch the corresponding event data efficiently.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use lists for ordered data, especially recent-N windows and simple queues. Always define a retention limit for feeds and a failure strategy for queues if jobs cannot simply disappear after a worker failure.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The structure answers 'what items are at the ends and in this order?' rather than 'which members have scores?' If ranking or uniqueness becomes central, another structure is a better fit.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Left/right push and pop operations create queue or stack behavior. Blocking list operations allow workers to wait for work. Bounded lists are especially important for feeds and histories so retention is explicit.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not create unbounded activity lists. Do not assume a basic pop-based queue automatically gives reliable acknowledgement and retry semantics.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interviewers may ask list versus stream. A list is a simple ordered collection and can implement lightweight queues, while Redis Streams provide IDs, consumer groups, replay-oriented workflows, and richer delivery tracking.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A notification worker consumes image-processing jobs from a list. If jobs are business-critical, the team adds a recovery strategy or chooses Streams/a dedicated queue rather than relying on a blind pop.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: LPUSH/RPUSH, LPOP/RPOP, blocking pops, trimming, Streams, queues, idempotency, and retries.

topics.title: Sets
topics.description: Unique membership, set algebra, tags, permissions, and relationship modeling.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis sets represent unique members. Their native semantics make membership tests and set algebra direct operations, which is useful for tags, permissions, cohorts, and relationships.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A Redis set stores unique members, so membership rather than position is the central operation. This makes sets a strong fit for permissions, tags, group membership, feature enrollment, and relationship lists where duplicates have no meaning. Set algebra adds another advantage: intersections answer “members common to both groups,” unions combine memberships, and differences express exclusion. Because the structure represents uniqueness directly, the application does not need to sort or deduplicate a list just to answer a membership question. Sets can also serve as feature rollout groups, such as a set of user IDs allowed to try a new checkout flow. The modeling question is whether the application cares about order. If order is essential, a list or sorted set may be more appropriate. If the primary questions are “is this member present?” or “what members are shared?” a set is usually a natural representation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Keep `team:platform` and `team:security` as sets of employee IDs. Their intersection gives employees who belong to both teams. A separate `feature:fast-checkout` set can contain user IDs enrolled in a rollout.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use sets when uniqueness and membership are the main requirements. If you later need ordering or a numeric score, reconsider the structure instead of forcing the set to simulate a ranking.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The set encodes uniqueness as part of the data model. Adding the same member again does not create another logical membership.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Use SADD/SREM/SISMEMBER for membership and SMEMBERS or incremental scanning when enumeration is actually needed. Intersections, unions, and differences can answer relationship questions without client-side deduplication.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Large sets can still be expensive to enumerate. Avoid treating SMEMBERS on a massive set as a harmless read simply because membership checks are efficient.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interview questions often compare sets and sorted sets. Choose a set when uniqueness and membership matter; choose a sorted set when each member also needs a numeric ordering score.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A feature rollout stores enrolled user IDs in a set. Authorization checks use SISMEMBER on the request path while administrative reports use incremental scanning rather than dumping the whole set.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: SADD, SISMEMBER, SINTER, SUNION, SDIFF, sorted sets, ACL modeling, cohorts, and SCAN.

topics.title: Sorted Sets
topics.description: Unique members with numeric scores, ranking, score ranges, and dynamic ordering.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Sorted sets combine unique members with numeric scores. The score supplies an ordering signal, making the structure ideal for leaderboards, priorities, popularity, scheduling windows, and ranked feeds.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A sorted set combines unique members with numeric scores. The score determines ordering, which makes the structure particularly useful for leaderboards, reputation, popularity, priorities, and other ranked views. Unlike a manually maintained position number, the rank is derived from the current score, so updating a member's score naturally changes its position. Applications can also query ranges based on score or retrieve members by rank. The design should distinguish the member identity from the score meaning: a member might be a player ID while the score is points, or an item ID while the score represents a popularity calculation. Ties and score-update rules should be defined at the application level so the displayed ranking is deterministic when required. Sorted sets are valuable because the data structure itself captures the relationship between an entity and the number used to order it.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A coding game keeps `leaderboard:weekly` with players and scores: player 17 → 1840, player 22 → 2115, player 31 → 1975. When player 17 earns points, only the score needs to change; the ordering is recalculated by Redis's sorted-set machinery.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use sorted sets when the application repeatedly asks for top-N members, rank, or score ranges. Keep the score definition stable and document how ties are displayed to users.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The score is the ordering index, while the member is the identity. Changing the score changes where the member appears without changing the member itself.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Scores can be updated without rebuilding the collection. Applications can query by rank or score range, retrieve top-N results, and remove members independently. Tie behavior should be understood and made deterministic at the presentation layer when required.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not store a score whose meaning changes without a migration or recalculation plan. Watch large range queries and hot ranking updates.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Be ready to compare sorted sets with sets and lists. A sorted set is appropriate when every member participates in a numeric ordering; it is not simply a faster list.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A gaming platform maintains a weekly leaderboard in a sorted set. The API asks for the top 20 and the player's rank; profile details remain in another structure or database.

topics.title: Choosing the Right Data Structure
topics.description: A practical decision process for selecting Redis structures from application operations.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Choosing the Right Data Structure is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. Redis features are easiest to use well when the access pattern, lifecycle, consistency requirement, and failure behavior are explicit.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Structure selection should begin with the application's dominant operations, not with the names of Redis data types. A scalar value or complete cache entry points toward a string. Independently mutable object fields point toward a hash. Ordered recent data or a simple queue points toward a list. Unique membership and set algebra point toward a set. Member-plus-score ranking points toward a sorted set. The same application can and often should use several structures at once. A profile may be a hash, its recent actions a list, permissions a set, and reputation a sorted-set member. A common mistake is to force all data for one entity into one large structure even when the required operations are fundamentally different. Good modeling also considers lifecycle, cardinality, update frequency, consistency, and network access. The best structure is the one that makes the important operations direct while keeping state understandable and maintainable.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For a fitness application: `profile:user:7` can be a hash, `recent:workouts:7` a list, `badges:user:7` a set, and `ranking:weekly` a sorted set. No single structure is responsible for every feature.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Write down the top five read and write operations before designing keys. For each, identify the desired latency, collection size, ordering requirement, uniqueness requirement, and update pattern, then choose the simplest matching structure.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Big O notation describes how an operation's work grows as the relevant amount of data grows. It is a planning tool, not a precise stopwatch. Constant-style O(1) behavior is attractive for direct membership or simple access; O(log N) grows slowly and commonly appears in ordered operations; O(N) means the work can grow in proportion to the collection or keyspace. Some commands have terms such as O(log N + M), where N is the search structure and M is the number of returned or processed elements. Sorting-style work may contain additional factors. The most important Redis lesson is to identify what N actually represents. A command that is harmless on a collection of 50 items may become a production problem on 20 million items. Complexity should therefore be evaluated together with cardinality, frequency, command blocking behavior, and network cost.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If a request scans a collection of 8 million members, the fact that each comparison is cheap does not make the operation harmless. A direct lookup that remains roughly constant-style is usually far safer for a hot request path than repeatedly traversing millions of elements.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: For every hot command, ask what grows: number of keys, members, returned results, or sorted items. Combine Big O reasoning with production measurements and worst-case cardinality rather than relying on a benchmark with tiny data.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Redis is primarily organized around keys and explicit structures rather than arbitrary relational predicates. When the application needs multiple ways to find the same object, model each important access path deliberately. topics.title: References and Indexes
topics.description: ID references, manually maintained indexes, stale data, and cleanup design.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: References and Indexes is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: References store identifiers that point to objects held elsewhere. This is useful for recent-item lists, relationship sets, category membership, and manual indexes because the full object is stored once. The design resembles normalized data modeling: one canonical record plus multiple lightweight access paths. The advantage is reduced duplication and easier object updates. The cost is that references can become broken or stale. If `product:88` is deleted while `featured:products` still contains `88`, a later read encounters a dangling reference. In critical workflows, updates to the object and its indexes may need transactional or scripted treatment. References are not automatically maintained by Redis just because they look like relationships; the application owns their correctness.

sections.content: `recent:orders:42` might contain order IDs 700, 701, and 705, while `order:700`, `order:701`, and `order:705` hold the details. Deleting order 701 requires a policy for removing or tolerating its old reference.

topics.description: Network latency, multi-key commands, pipelining, batch sizing, and throughput.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Round Trips is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A Redis command is executed on a server, but the client and server still have to communicate. When latency between them is nontrivial, repeatedly sending one command, waiting, and sending the next can dominate the cost of otherwise fast operations. Multi-key commands can retrieve or update several independent values in one request when the data model allows it. Pipelining does not automatically make commands atomic; it is primarily a communication optimization. Transactions and scripts solve different problems.

topics.title: Transactions
topics.description: Atomic commands, MULTI/EXEC, DISCARD, ordering, WATCH, optimistic concurrency, and retries.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis transactions coordinate a sequence of commands using MULTI and EXEC. WATCH adds optimistic concurrency control by aborting execution when watched keys change before EXEC.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Redis commands are individually atomic, but some business operations require several changes to be treated as one coordinated unit. `MULTI` queues commands and `EXEC` executes the queued sequence in order; `DISCARD` abandons a queued transaction. This is useful when several related updates should not be interleaved with other Redis command execution. `WATCH` provides optimistic concurrency control: the client watches keys, reads the current state, calculates a new value, queues its write, and attempts `EXEC`. If a watched key changed before execution, the transaction attempt can fail, allowing the application to retry or abort. This pattern is useful for conditional updates but can suffer from contention if many clients repeatedly modify the same hot key. Retry limits and backoff should therefore be part of the design. Transactions provide coordination semantics; they are not a replacement for durable business transactions in a relational system.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Suppose a seat inventory value is 1. Two clients read it. With optimistic concurrency, each watches the relevant key before calculating its update. If one client changes the key first, the other's transaction attempt detects the conflict instead of blindly overwriting the newer state.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use a transaction when multiple Redis updates form one logical operation. Use WATCH for conditional read-modify-write behavior, and use a small retry policy so contention cannot create an uncontrolled retry storm.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of WATCH as a lightweight optimistic lock. The client reads state, derives an update, and asks Redis to commit only if the watched state remained unchanged.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: MULTI queues commands rather than immediately applying each queued command. EXEC runs the transaction's queued commands in order. WATCH is useful for compare-and-set workflows where the application must calculate a new value from a current value.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: High contention can cause repeated WATCH retries. Also do not describe MULTI/EXEC as rollback-capable database transactions with arbitrary isolation levels.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Know the difference between a transaction, pipeline, and Lua script: a pipeline reduces network round trips; MULTI/EXEC provides grouped execution semantics; a script can perform server-side conditional logic without returning intermediate state to the client.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A seat-allocation service watches the remaining-seat key, computes a new count, and retries a bounded number of times if another client changes the key first.

topics.title: KEYS Anti-Pattern
topics.description: Why whole-keyspace discovery can block work and how explicit structures and SCAN help.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: KEYS Anti-Pattern is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A whole-keyspace pattern search is convenient during small experiments but dangerous as a normal production request. A broad `KEYS` operation may inspect a very large number of keys in one server-side operation, so its work grows with the entire keyspace rather than the small result the application actually wants. The safe principle is to model common application queries directly and reserve broad discovery for controlled administrative tasks.

sections.content: Instead of searching millions of keys for all alerts belonging to tenant 91, maintain `alerts:tenant:91` containing alert IDs. A request can read that structure directly. An operator who truly needs to inspect cache keys can use incremental scanning outside the hot request path.

topics.title: Expiration and TTL
topics.description: Temporary data, relative and absolute expiration, cache-aside behavior, and lifecycle design.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Expiration and TTL is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Expiration gives temporary data an explicit lifetime. A cache entry, session, reset token, or rate-limit record can be created with a TTL so the application does not need a separate cleanup process for every expired item. Relative expiration expresses a duration, while absolute expiration expresses a target time. TTL inspection helps diagnose whether an entry is approaching expiry, and removing expiration is possible when the application's lifecycle changes. Expiration should be part of the data model, not an afterthought: a cache without a lifecycle can grow indefinitely, while a business record given an accidental short TTL can disappear unexpectedly. Cache-aside is a common pattern: read the cache, use it on a hit, and on a miss load the authoritative source, store the result, attach a suitable lifetime, and return it. TTLs should reflect freshness requirements and acceptable recomputation cost.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A product recommendation response may be cached under `cache:recommendations:42` for 120 seconds. A password-reset token might have a much shorter lifetime. The two keys both expire, but their durations come from different business rules.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: For every expiring key, document why it expires, what happens after a miss, and whether expiration should be refreshed on access. Never use TTL as a substitute for backup or durable storage.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A list can implement a lightweight work queue by placing jobs at one end and consuming them from the other. This is attractive for small systems because the data model is easy to understand and blocking consumption can let workers wait efficiently for new jobs. The right question is not whether Redis can hold jobs, but whether the delivery semantics match the business requirement. For transient internal work, a simple list may be enough; for critical workflows, additional structures or a dedicated messaging system may be appropriate.

sections.content: A thumbnail service can put `resize:img:501`, `resize:img:502`, and `resize:img:503` into a queue. Workers block while waiting for work, take jobs, process them, and record completion according to the application's reliability policy.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Pub/sub is a broadcast communication model. A publisher sends a message to a channel, and all currently interested subscribers receive it. Pattern subscriptions can allow a subscriber to listen to families of channel names. This is useful for real-time notifications such as dashboard updates, lightweight application events, or live status signals. The important architectural distinction is delivery semantics: pub/sub is not the same as a durable work queue. A subscriber that is not listening at the relevant time may not receive a transient message, so pub/sub should not automatically be chosen for events that must be recoverable. Queue consumers typically compete for work, while pub/sub intentionally broadcasts one event to multiple listeners. Channel naming should reflect event ownership and domain boundaries so subscribers do not needlessly receive unrelated traffic.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A deployment dashboard subscribes to `ops:events` and receives messages such as “service restarted.” A notification service and a monitoring UI can both listen to the same channel because both are interested in the event.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use pub/sub for low-latency notifications where transient delivery is acceptable. If every event must be replayable or acknowledged, choose a durable event/queue design instead of assuming pub/sub provides persistence.

topics.description: Cursor-based incremental iteration, COUNT hints, duplicate handling, changing keyspaces, and HSCAN/SSCAN/ZSCAN.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: SCAN is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: `SCAN` provides incremental iteration through the keyspace using a cursor. The client starts from cursor 0, receives another cursor plus a batch of results, and continues until Redis returns cursor 0 again. The requested `COUNT` is a hint, not a promise that exactly that many items will appear. A batch may even contain no matching items while the returned cursor is nonzero, so an empty response is not proof that iteration has finished. Iteration can also expose duplicates and is not an immutable snapshot when keys are added or removed during the scan. These properties mean the application should make processing idempotent or otherwise tolerate repeated observations when necessary. The same incremental pattern is available for hashes, sets, and sorted sets through their corresponding scan commands. SCAN is therefore safer for large maintenance jobs than demanding a complete keyspace traversal at once, but it still consumes server resources.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A maintenance worker needs to find cache keys matching `cache:session:*`. It repeatedly scans with a moderate count hint, processes returned keys, and continues until the cursor becomes zero. It does not stop merely because one batch is empty.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use SCAN for controlled discovery and maintenance. Make the processing safe to repeat, bound the work per iteration, and avoid turning a full keyspace scan into a synchronous user request.

topics.title: Lua Scripting
topics.description: Server-side conditional logic, EVAL/EVALSHA, KEYS versus ARGV, atomicity, and script performance.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Lua scripts move compact decision logic into Redis so reads, checks, and writes can happen together without repeated client/server round trips. Redis executes a script atomically relative to other commands, which is powerful but can block unrelated work if the script runs too long.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Lua scripting lets application logic execute close to the Redis data it operates on. This is useful when a business operation needs a read, a condition, and one or more writes to happen together without multiple client/server round trips. `EVAL` executes a script, while a loaded script can later be invoked through its SHA identifier with `EVALSHA`. Script inputs are separated into `KEYS` for Redis keys and `ARGV` for ordinary values. This distinction is important for clarity and for deployments where Redis needs to understand key placement. A focused script can implement operations such as “decrease inventory only when enough stock exists.” Scripts execute atomically relative to other Redis commands, but that strength has a cost: a long-running script can delay unrelated work. Lua should therefore contain narrow, predictable logic rather than large scans or entire application workflows. Script management commands are operational tools and should be used deliberately.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: For stock key `stock:keyboard`, a script can read the current quantity, compare it with the requested amount, decrement only when sufficient stock exists, and return success or failure. The client sends the requested quantity as an argument instead of embedding it into the script source.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use scripts for compact read-check-write operations that need atomic behavior or fewer round trips. Keep them short, test them with edge cases, and monitor their execution time.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Use scripting when atomic conditional behavior cannot be expressed cleanly with a single command or a WATCH-based workflow would cause too much contention or network chatter.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Pass Redis keys through KEYS and ordinary parameters through ARGV. Keep scripts deterministic, bounded, and focused on the data they need. Modern Redis deployments may also use function-based server-side logic, so version-specific documentation matters.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Never put unbounded scans, expensive loops, or entire application workflows into a script. A script's atomicity does not make an expensive algorithm cheap.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: An inventory script can read stock, reject a purchase when insufficient, otherwise decrement stock and return a status code. The client sends the inventory key through KEYS and the requested quantity through ARGV.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A checkout service uses a short inventory reservation script, monitors script latency, tests failure paths, and keeps the script versioned with application code.

topics.title: Authentication and Command Security
topics.description: Authentication versus authorization, administrative commands, command restrictions, and defense in depth.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis security has multiple layers: network reachability, authentication, authorization, encryption, command permissions, and operational access. Modern Redis supports ACL-based identities and command/key permissions, while older password-only patterns are more limited.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Authentication answers who is connecting; authorization answers what that identity is allowed to do. The supplied material describes an older password-oriented security model and defensive techniques such as restricting dangerous administrative commands. These ideas are useful for understanding the security boundary, but command renaming alone should never be treated as a complete protection mechanism. A secure deployment should combine authentication with network isolation, least privilege, protected administrative access, and careful exposure of the Redis port. Destructive operations deserve special attention because an operator or compromised client with broad permissions can remove large portions of the dataset. Security settings should also be reviewed when Redis is upgraded because modern releases may provide different and more granular mechanisms than the older model described by the material.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A production service should not expose Redis directly to the public internet. Application clients receive only the permissions they need, while administrative access is restricted to trusted operational paths. A destructive command is not considered safe merely because its default name has been changed.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Treat network reachability, authentication, authorization, encryption where appropriate, and administrative access as separate controls. Review security configuration during deployment and upgrades rather than relying on a single command-level trick.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Treat Redis as an internal privileged system, not a harmless cache endpoint. A stolen credential can expose or destroy large amounts of application state.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Design security around least privilege rather than relying on renamed commands or obscurity. Restrict who can reach Redis, authenticate clients, grant only required command/key access, protect credentials, and use TLS where the deployment requires encrypted transport.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Never commit Redis credentials to source control, expose the default port broadly, or assume authentication alone protects against an over-privileged account.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interviewers often ask whether Redis should be exposed publicly, what ACLs solve, and whether disabling or renaming dangerous commands is enough. The answer should emphasize defense in depth.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A multi-service platform gives each service an ACL identity scoped to the key families it needs, isolates Redis at the network layer, rotates credentials, and audits administrative access.

topics.title: Replication
topics.description: Primary-replica copying, read scaling, replication lag, redundancy, and why replicas are not backups.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Replication creates copies of a primary dataset on replicas. It supports redundancy and can support read scaling, but replication is asynchronous in common deployments and therefore can expose lag.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Replication creates additional live copies of Redis data by propagating changes from a primary to replicas. Replicas can improve redundancy and may serve reads in architectures where slightly stale results are acceptable. They do not automatically eliminate replication lag: after a primary changes from one value to another, a replica may temporarily expose the previous state. Applications that require read-after-write consistency should therefore be deliberate about where reads go. Replication also is not the same as backup. If an accidental deletion reaches the primary and is replicated, the replicas can reproduce the same bad state. A backup provides a historical recovery point, while replication primarily provides another live copy. Failover is another separate concern: having a replica does not by itself define how clients discover and promote a replacement primary when the original fails.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A read-heavy catalog service may send writes to the primary and distribute cache-friendly reads across replicas. If a user changes a preference and immediately reads it back, the application must account for the possibility that a replica has not received the update yet.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use replicas for redundancy and appropriate read scaling, but document acceptable staleness and failover behavior. Pair replication with independent backups when historical recovery is required.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The mental model is 'live redundancy' rather than 'time machine.' A replica helps survive some live failures, while a backup helps recover from corruption, deletion, or historical mistakes.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Applications must decide whether stale reads are acceptable and where read-after-write traffic should go. Failover requires an architecture such as Sentinel or another managed control plane; a replica by itself is not an automatic failover system.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not promise zero data loss from asynchronous replication. Do not assume every read from a replica is immediately consistent with the latest write.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Explain the difference between replication and backup: replication copies current state, so an accidental deletion can propagate; backup preserves historical recovery points.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A read-heavy service writes to the primary and sends safe-to-stale reads to replicas. Critical read-after-write operations are routed deliberately, and failover behavior is tested.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Backups is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. Redis features are easiest to use well when the access pattern, lifecycle, consistency requirement, and failure behavior are explicit.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A backup is designed to recover data from an earlier safe state. That makes it fundamentally different from a live replica. Snapshot files can be copied to another machine, backup system, or object-storage environment so that a host failure does not destroy both the active dataset and its only recovery copy. Backup frequency should follow the recovery point objective: if losing an hour is unacceptable, a daily backup is insufficient. Recovery point quality is not enough by itself; the team must also know how to restore, validate the recovered dataset, and return the application to service. A replica may assist with persistence work in some architectures, but it should not be considered the historical backup policy. Backup retention, off-host storage, encryption, access control, and restoration testing are part of the complete recovery design.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A subscription service keeps periodic snapshots and copies them outside the Redis host. If the host is lost, the team can create a replacement instance and restore from the most recent safe snapshot instead of depending on a surviving local disk.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Define RPO and RTO, store backups away from the primary host, protect backup access, retain multiple recovery points when needed, and perform restoration drills rather than assuming that a successful backup job guarantees recovery.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Build the mental model around four questions: what state does Redis maintain, what operation does the application need, what work does the server perform, and what happens when the workload becomes large or a node fails? For Backups, a convenient command is not automatically a good production design. The surrounding data model and operational policy determine whether the feature remains predictable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: explain Backups in terms of the problem it solves, the relevant command or data structure, expected complexity or latency behavior, and the main trade-offs. A strong answer also compares it with the closest alternative and gives one production failure mode. Avoid command-only answers; explain why the design is appropriate.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls with Backups include choosing it without defining the access pattern, ignoring collection size or response size, assuming Redis provides stronger consistency or durability than configured, and overlooking retries, expiration, or failure behavior. Test boundary cases explicitly and document the assumptions that make the design safe.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Backups when its native semantics directly match the workload and its operational cost is bounded. Avoid it when the same requirement can be served more simply, when the data must support arbitrary querying that Redis does not model directly, or when the feature's failure semantics do not satisfy the business requirement.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: In production, treat Backups as part of an observable design. Define ownership of the keys, expected cardinality, latency target, error/retry behavior, memory impact, monitoring signals, and recovery procedure. Load-test realistic data sizes and include failure scenarios before making the feature a critical dependency.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include Redis key naming, data structures, command complexity, pipelining, transactions, expiration, persistence, replication, observability, and capacity planning. Connect Backups to neighboring Redis features rather than learning it as an isolated command.

topics.shortDescription: Recovery points, snapshot copying, off-host storage, and separating backup from replication.

topics.title: Redis Streams
topics.description: Append-only event records with IDs, consumer groups, pending entries, acknowledgements, replay, and event-processing workflows.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis Streams provide an append-oriented record structure with generated or client-supplied IDs. They are designed for event and message workflows where consumers may need ordered records, acknowledgements, replay, and consumer-group coordination.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: An entry contains field-value pairs and an ID. Producers add entries with XADD; consumers can read ranges or, with consumer groups, claim work as part of a coordinated processing model. Stream length and retention should be bounded when business history does not need to grow forever.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An order service can append `order.created` events to `orders:events`. A notification worker and analytics worker can consume the same stream independently, each maintaining its own progress.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use Streams when the application needs durable-in-Redis event records, replay-oriented consumption, or consumer groups. For transient broadcast notifications, pub/sub is simpler; for very large event ecosystems, compare Redis with a dedicated log platform.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of a Stream as a growing sequence of records plus metadata that lets consumers reason about position and pending work. It is more than a list because the ID and consumer-group machinery make processing state explicit.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Know XADD, XREAD, XREADGROUP, XACK, XPENDING, XCLAIM/claiming concepts, trimming, IDs, consumer groups, and the distinction from lists and pub/sub.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not let streams grow without a retention plan. Do not treat reading a message as equivalent to successful processing; acknowledgement and retry behavior matter.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Redis Streams when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production systems should define retention, consumer lag, pending-entry recovery, idempotency, poison-message handling, and monitoring. Test what happens when a consumer dies after receiving but before acknowledging a message.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include consumer groups, pending entries, acknowledgement, idempotency, retries, pub/sub, lists, persistence, and event-driven architecture.

topics.title: Consumer Groups
topics.description: Stream consumer groups, message ownership, XREADGROUP, acknowledgements, pending entries, retries, and recovery.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Consumer groups let multiple consumers cooperate on a Redis Stream so entries can be assigned to consumers while the group tracks delivery and pending work. This supports worker-style processing rather than broadcasting every entry to every worker.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: XREADGROUP reads on behalf of a named group and consumer. A successful processing workflow normally acknowledges an entry with XACK. Pending entries expose work delivered but not yet acknowledged, which creates a recovery path when a consumer fails.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A payment-event worker group has three consumers. Each processes assigned stream entries, acknowledges successful work, and periodically inspects pending entries so work abandoned by a crashed consumer can be recovered according to the retry policy.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use consumer groups when work should be distributed among workers while the stream remains a shared event source. Do not use them merely because multiple services need the same event; separate groups may be more appropriate for independent processing.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The key mental model is group-level progress plus per-consumer ownership. An entry can be delivered to a consumer and remain pending until acknowledged, so failure handling is part of normal design.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers may ask how Redis Streams differ from lists, what XACK does, why pending entries exist, and how a crashed consumer's messages are recovered.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not assume XACK means the business operation is globally committed. Make processing idempotent because retries can occur, and monitor pending counts and consumer lag.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Consumer Groups when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Run consumers with stable identities, bounded concurrency, retry limits, poison-message handling, and observability for pending entries. Recovery procedures should be tested rather than invented during an incident.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include Redis Streams, XREADGROUP, XACK, XPENDING, consumer lag, idempotency, retries, dead-letter handling, and event processing.

topics.title: Redis Sentinel
topics.description: Monitoring, automatic failover, primary discovery, replicas, quorum, and client behavior in non-clustered HA deployments.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Sentinel is a high-availability mechanism for Redis primary-replica deployments. It monitors instances, helps detect failures, coordinates failover, and provides a way for clients to discover the current primary.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Sentinel is not a sharding system. It is primarily about monitoring and failover for a replicated topology. Quorum and the number of Sentinel processes matter because failure decisions should not depend on one isolated observer.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A service has one primary and two replicas watched by multiple Sentinel processes. When the primary fails, the Sentinel deployment can coordinate promotion of a replica and clients configured for Sentinel can discover the new primary.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use Sentinel when you need HA for a non-clustered primary-replica topology. If the dataset itself must be partitioned across nodes, Redis Cluster or a managed service may be the better architecture.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think of Sentinel as the control plane that answers 'which node should be primary now?' It does not magically make application writes durable or eliminate replication lag.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Know the difference between Sentinel and Cluster, how failover affects clients, and why quorum is a control-plane decision rather than a data-consistency guarantee.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not claim Sentinel provides zero data loss or that a replica is always current. Test client reconnect behavior and understand what happens to writes around a failover.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Redis Sentinel when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production operations should monitor Sentinel health, replication lag, failover duration, client errors, and the state of promoted replicas. Run controlled failover drills.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include replication, failover, quorum, Redis Cluster, client discovery, RPO/RTO, and high availability.

topics.title: Redis Cluster
topics.description: Slot-based sharding, replicas, cluster-aware clients, resharding, cross-slot constraints, and cluster failure behavior.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis Cluster distributes keyspace ownership across hash slots and combines partitioning with replica-based failure handling. It is designed for horizontal scale when one Redis server is no longer sufficient for the dataset or throughput.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Clients normally route commands to the node owning the relevant slot. Multi-key operations have placement constraints, so related keys may need compatible key names and hash tags when the operation must be handled on one shard.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: An application stores `user:{42}` and `cart:{42}` so the `{42}` hash tag can place both keys in the same slot when a supported multi-key operation needs co-location.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use Cluster when partitioning and horizontal scale are real requirements. Do not introduce it solely because 'distributed' sounds more scalable; the operational and modeling complexity is significant.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The cluster changes locality: the key determines which node owns the state. A correct data model therefore includes placement requirements, not only logical relationships.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers often ask about hash slots, MOVED/ASK redirections, replicas, resharding, and why arbitrary cross-slot multi-key commands are constrained.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not assume Cluster fixes hot keys, and do not casually perform cross-slot operations. Test resharding, node failures, client routing, and key distribution with production-like traffic.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Redis Cluster when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production clusters need cluster-aware clients, slot-distribution monitoring, replica health, failover testing, resharding procedures, and capacity headroom on every shard.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include hash slots, hash tags, sharding, replicas, resharding, Sentinel, hot keys, and cluster-aware clients.

topics.title: Eviction Policies
topics.description: maxmemory, eviction policy choices, volatile versus all-keys behavior, cache design, and capacity boundaries.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Eviction determines what Redis may remove when configured memory limits are reached. This is central to cache design because the policy defines which data can disappear under pressure.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: maxmemory establishes a memory boundary, while the selected policy determines whether Redis evicts any key, only keys with expiration, or uses access/frequency signals. Exact policy behavior is version- and configuration-dependent, so deployments should verify current documentation.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A product-cache deployment chooses a policy appropriate for disposable cache entries and gives cached keys expirations. When memory pressure rises, Redis can reclaim eligible entries instead of allowing unbounded growth.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use eviction for intentionally disposable data such as caches. Avoid relying on eviction to protect authoritative business state unless the data model explicitly tolerates loss and the configured policy guarantees the required behavior.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The mental model is 'memory is a bounded resource and eviction is a data-loss policy.' Once that is understood, choosing a policy becomes a business decision rather than a tuning checkbox.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Be prepared to compare noeviction-style behavior with eviction strategies and to explain why TTL-based eligibility matters for volatile policies.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common mistakes include mixing authoritative and disposable data in one eviction domain, setting maxmemory without headroom, and assuming eviction is predictable enough to replace application-level lifecycle rules.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Eviction Policies when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production monitoring should track memory, evictions, hit rate, rejected writes, and key TTL distribution. Load-test memory pressure and verify that eviction affects only data the application can rebuild.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include maxmemory, TTL, cache-aside, cache hit rate, memory fragmentation, capacity planning, and persistence.

topics.title: Cache-Aside Pattern
topics.description: Cache-aside reads and writes, invalidation, TTLs, stale data, cache misses, and authoritative database boundaries.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Cache-aside keeps the authoritative record in a primary data store while Redis holds a derived copy. Reads check Redis first; misses load the source, populate Redis, and return the result.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: The design must define invalidation and freshness. A write can update the source and then invalidate or refresh the cache. TTL provides a safety boundary but does not automatically guarantee immediate consistency.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A product API reads `cache:product:42`; on a miss it loads product 42 from the database, stores a serialized response with a suitable TTL, and returns it. A product update invalidates the cache key.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use cache-aside for read-heavy data that can be rebuilt. Avoid it for state where serving stale or missing data violates the business requirement unless the consistency policy is explicitly designed.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The cache is a materialized view, not the authority. This mental model explains why cache misses are normal, invalidation is hard, and rebuilding must always be possible.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers may ask cache-aside versus write-through/write-behind, how to prevent stale data, and what happens when the database succeeds but cache invalidation fails.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Never assume invalidation is perfectly reliable. Handle stampedes, serialization failures, stale values, backend overload during mass misses, and partial outages.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Cache-Aside Pattern when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production systems should monitor hit ratio, miss latency, backend load, invalidation failures, stale-read indicators, and cache memory. Use bounded TTLs and controlled refresh strategies.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include TTL, cache stampede, write-through caching, invalidation, consistency, serialization, and database load.
