topics.title: Cache Stampede Prevention
topics.description: Preventing synchronized cache misses with jitter, request coalescing, locking, stale-while-revalidate, and bounded refresh work.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A cache stampede occurs when many requests miss or simultaneously refresh the same hot key, causing a burst against Redis and especially the authoritative backend. Prevention reduces synchronized refresh work.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Useful techniques include TTL jitter, request coalescing, short-lived locks, stale-while-revalidate behavior, and proactive refresh. Each technique changes freshness and failure semantics, so it should be chosen from the workload rather than copied as a universal recipe.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A homepage cache expires at roughly the same time for thousands of requests. Adding randomized TTL jitter spreads refreshes, while a single-flight mechanism ensures only one request rebuilds the expensive value.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use stampede protection for expensive, highly popular keys with synchronized expiry. Avoid complex locking when the value is cheap to rebuild; unnecessary coordination can become a new bottleneck.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The core idea is to control concurrency around regeneration, not merely increase Redis capacity. The backend is often the component that suffers most from a simultaneous miss.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Know cache stampede, cache avalanche, TTL jitter, single-flight/request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, and distributed-lock trade-offs.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not make every cache refresh wait on one global lock. Avoid unbounded lock retries and ensure stale or missing data has a defined fallback.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Cache Stampede Prevention when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production systems combine jitter, bounded regeneration time, backend rate limits, observability, and graceful stale serving where business rules allow it.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include cache-aside, TTL, distributed locks, rate limiting, request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, and backend protection.

topics.title: Distributed Locks
topics.description: Lock acquisition, unique tokens, expiration, safe release, contention, failure modes, and when a lock is actually needed.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: A Redis-based distributed lock attempts to ensure that only one participant performs a critical operation at a time across processes or machines. Correctness depends on unique ownership tokens, expiration, and safe release.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A common single-instance pattern uses a unique random token and an atomic conditional set with expiration. Release should verify that the stored token still belongs to the caller before deleting it, so one process cannot accidentally remove another process's lock.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: Worker A acquires `lock:report:42` with a unique token and short lease. If A finishes, it releases only when the token still matches. If A crashes, the lease eventually expires so another worker can proceed.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use a Redis lock for bounded coordination where temporary lock loss or retry can be handled safely. Avoid treating a simple lock as a universal substitute for database constraints or a consensus system.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The lock is a lease, not a magical ownership certificate. Expiration means ownership can end while the original process still believes it is working, so the protected operation must tolerate that possibility.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers often test SET NX EX semantics, unique tokens, safe unlock, expiration, retries, and whether a lock provides exactly-once execution.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not delete a lock blindly by key. Do not hold locks indefinitely, and do not assume a lock prevents all duplicate work if the holder pauses past its lease.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Distributed Locks when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production designs use short bounded leases, safe release logic, metrics for contention and expiry, idempotent operations, and a clear decision about whether stronger coordination is required.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include SET NX, TTL, Lua, transactions, idempotency, leases, fencing tokens, leader election, and database constraints.

topics.title: HyperLogLog
topics.description: Approximate distinct counting, PFADD, PFCOUNT, PF merge behavior, memory efficiency, and accuracy trade-offs.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: HyperLogLog is a probabilistic Redis structure for estimating cardinality, such as the approximate number of unique visitors, while using far less memory than storing every unique identifier.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: PFADD adds observations, PFCOUNT estimates cardinality, and PFMERGE combines sketches. The result is an estimate rather than an exact membership set, so it should be used when approximate counts are acceptable.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A media site records anonymous visitor IDs into a daily HyperLogLog. The product reports approximate unique visitors without storing a full set containing every ID.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use HyperLogLog for large-scale approximate distinct counts. Avoid it when exact membership, exact cardinality, or the ability to enumerate members is required.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The key mental model is a compact statistical sketch: it remembers enough information to estimate cardinality but intentionally does not preserve the original member list.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers may ask HyperLogLog versus SET. The set gives exact unique membership but consumes memory proportional to members; HyperLogLog gives a compact approximate count without enumeration.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not use HyperLogLog to answer 'is this exact user present?' and do not present an estimate as an exact business number without explaining the error characteristics.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use HyperLogLog when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production use should document acceptable error, aggregation boundaries, retention, and the consequences of approximate reporting.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE, sets, cardinality estimation, analytics, and memory efficiency.

topics.title: Bitmaps
topics.description: Bit-oriented state, SETBIT, GETBIT, BITCOUNT, compact boolean flags, and high-cardinality event tracking.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis bitmaps use string bits as compact boolean or bit-oriented state. They are useful when the application maps many integer positions to on/off properties or counts.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: SETBIT changes one bit at an offset, GETBIT reads it, and BITCOUNT counts set bits. Offsets can become large, so capacity planning should consider the highest offset and the resulting string size.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A learning platform assigns each day a bit position for a user's attendance history. A set bit means the learner was active that day, and BITCOUNT can answer how many tracked days were active.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use bitmaps for dense integer-indexed boolean state and efficient aggregate bit counts. Avoid them when IDs are sparse, semantics are complex, or the bit position mapping would be difficult to maintain.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The bitmap is an array of bits addressed by offset. It is compact because many boolean values share bytes instead of requiring one key or string token per state.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers may compare bitmaps with sets: sets are natural for sparse identifiers and membership; bitmaps can be dramatically more compact for dense numeric positions.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Watch offset growth, accidental huge offsets, and unclear mapping between business IDs and bit positions. Document the encoding so another engineer can interpret the bits.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Bitmaps when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production systems should define the offset mapping, expected maximum offset, retention strategy, and metrics for memory growth.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts include SETBIT, GETBIT, BITCOUNT, bit operations, sets, HyperLogLog, counters, and compact telemetry.

topics.title: Keyspace Notifications
topics.description: Server-generated key event notifications, configuration, expiration events, delivery limitations, and event-driven integrations.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Keyspace notifications allow Redis to publish events about selected key operations, including certain expiration and mutation events, when the feature is configured. They are useful for reactive integrations but are not a durable event log.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Notifications are emitted as server activity occurs and are delivered through pub/sub-style channels. Configuration determines which event categories are generated, and enabling them has overhead, so the event stream should be treated as operationally best-effort.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A service enables expiration notifications for a narrowly defined integration. When temporary workflow keys expire, a worker receives a signal and performs follow-up work while accepting that the notification itself is not the durable source of truth.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use notifications for lightweight reactions where missing an event can be tolerated or reconstructed. Avoid them as the only mechanism for critical business workflows that require replay or guaranteed delivery.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The notification says 'Redis observed this event,' not 'your business process is durably committed.' This distinction prevents accidental coupling between ephemeral server events and durable workflows.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers may ask what keyspace notifications are, whether they are enabled by default, and whether they replace Streams. Explain the transient pub/sub-style delivery model.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not build critical recovery logic around a notification that can be missed. Avoid enabling broad event categories without measuring the overhead.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Keyspace Notifications when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production use should scope event categories, monitor subscriber health, and keep an authoritative source or rebuild path for any important derived state.

sections.content: Related concepts include pub/sub, Streams, expiration, key events, event-driven architecture, and observability.

topics.title: Memory Fragmentation and Capacity
topics.description: Allocator fragmentation, resident memory, maxmemory, dataset growth, large values, and capacity headroom.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Memory capacity is affected by more than logical dataset size. Redis's allocator, freed objects, replication buffers, client buffers, large collections, and temporary operations can cause resident memory to exceed a simple payload calculation.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Capacity planning should track logical used memory and operating-system resident memory, fragmentation indicators, growth rate, object-size distributions, and headroom. The right response to high memory may be resizing, deleting disposable data, changing object shape, reducing fragmentation, or altering workload behavior.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A service reports 12 GB of logical Redis data but consumes substantially more resident memory. The team investigates allocator fragmentation, replicas, buffers, large values, and workload churn before concluding that every key must be deleted.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use memory metrics to plan capacity and detect abnormal growth. Avoid sizing a server by multiplying key count by average payload alone; that calculation omits important overhead.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The mental model is 'payload is only one layer of memory.' Data structures have representation costs, and operational processes temporarily consume memory too.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interviewers may ask why Redis memory usage can exceed the apparent dataset size and how fragmentation affects capacity planning.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not run at the absolute RAM limit. Do not assume TTL alone guarantees low memory if incoming data grows faster than expired data is reclaimed.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Use Memory Fragmentation and Capacity when the requirement explicitly needs the semantics described above and the workload can tolerate its operational trade-offs. Avoid it when a simpler Redis structure, a single atomic command, or a durable external system provides the required guarantee with less complexity.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production monitoring should alert on memory pressure, fragmentation, eviction/rejection behavior, growth rate, and replica/client buffers. Capacity tests should use realistic object churn.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Redis scaling can increase capacity vertically or distribute keys horizontally. Once data is partitioned, key placement becomes part of the application's architecture because multi-key operations may require keys to reside together.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Scaling can be vertical or horizontal. Vertical scaling increases the capacity of one machine, such as adding RAM or faster hardware. Horizontal scaling distributes data or work across multiple Redis instances. Partitioning assigns keys to different nodes, often using a hashing strategy. A naive modulo rule can create significant movement when the number of nodes changes because the divisor changes for many keys. Consistent-hashing concepts reduce movement during membership changes by placing nodes and keys into a shared logical space. Clustered deployments can provide structured partitioning, rebalancing, and failure handling, but distributed data introduces new concerns such as key placement, multi-key operations, and operational complexity. Scaling should therefore be driven by measured limits: memory, CPU, throughput, latency, dataset size, or availability requirements. Adding nodes without understanding the access pattern can simply move the bottleneck elsewhere.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: With three independent instances, a simplistic `hash(key) % 3` rule distributes keys. Adding a fourth node changes the calculation to `% 4`, potentially remapping many keys. A partitioning strategy designed for membership changes can reduce the amount of movement.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Identify the actual bottleneck before scaling. When horizontal partitioning is required, define key distribution, rebalancing behavior, cross-node operation constraints, monitoring, and failure recovery before production rollout.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: The key insight is that horizontal scaling changes the unit of failure and the unit of locality. A key is no longer merely an address; it also determines which node owns the data.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Hash-based partitioning can spread keys, while Redis Cluster provides a structured slot-based distribution model. Rebalancing changes placement, so the design must account for hotspots, large keys, client routing, and operational migration.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not assume adding nodes automatically improves a hot-key workload. One extremely popular key can remain a bottleneck even when total capacity is large.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: Interviewers frequently ask why modulo hashing remaps keys when node count changes and how Redis Cluster avoids a single monolithic keyspace. Explain logical slots, client routing, and the limits of cross-slot operations.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A large API uses Redis Cluster, monitors slot distribution and hot keys, chooses key names carefully, and uses hash tags when related keys must be co-located for supported multi-key operations.

topics.title: High Availability
topics.description: Failure tolerance, replicas, failover planning, and the distinction between redundancy and automatic recovery.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: High availability is the ability to continue useful service through component failures. It requires more than replicas: the system needs failure detection, promotion, client redirection, operational procedures, and explicit data-loss expectations.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: High availability means the application can continue operating when a component fails. Replication supplies alternate copies, but failover is the mechanism and operational process that makes a surviving node usable as the replacement for a failed primary. Read replicas alone do not guarantee write availability because the application must know where to send writes after failure. A complete design considers failure detection, promotion, client discovery, data loss expectations, split-brain risks, and recovery procedures. The exact mechanisms depend on the Redis version and deployment architecture, so older material should not be copied blindly into a modern environment. High availability should also be tested under realistic failure conditions rather than inferred from the presence of a second server. The goal is not merely to have another copy; it is to have a controlled path from failure to a functioning service.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: A checkout service has a primary and replicas. During a primary failure, the architecture needs a defined process for selecting a replacement, redirecting clients, and handling writes that may not have reached every replica before the failure.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Document the failover path, expected data-loss window, client behavior, monitoring signals, and rollback plan. Run failure drills so the operational procedure is as reliable as the topology.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Think in terms of a state machine: healthy primary → failure detected → replacement promoted → clients discover the new writer → old node is repaired and rejoined safely.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Redis Sentinel can monitor primary/replica deployments and coordinate failover, while Redis Cluster combines sharding with replica-based failover. Managed Redis services may provide their own control plane. The exact mechanism should match the deployment model and Redis version.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Do not claim that two Redis servers automatically provide HA. Do not ignore client behavior during failover or the possibility of writes not yet replicated.

sections.title: When to use / avoid
sections.content: An interview-ready HA answer should cover failure detection, quorum or control-plane behavior, promotion, client discovery, split-brain considerations, replication lag, and recovery of the failed node.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: A checkout platform runs failure drills, verifies client reconnection behavior, measures failover time, and documents what transactions may be lost during a primary failure.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: Sentinel, Cluster, replication, quorum, failover, client discovery, RPO/RTO, and split-brain risk.

topics.description: Starting with application questions, mapping each question to a structure, and managing derived state.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Access-pattern modeling means designing Redis state from the questions the application must answer. Start by listing concrete operations such as “get user by ID,” “get user by email,” “show the latest orders,” “check permission,” and “show top users.” Then choose structures that make each operation direct. This can require multiple representations: one canonical object plus indexes, recent-item lists, membership sets, and rankings. Data modeling should also consider whether results must be fresh, whether they can be rebuilt, how large collections can become, and whether operations may span multiple nodes in a scaled deployment. Redis rewards explicit design because the system does not automatically infer arbitrary secondary queries from generic application objects.

sections.content: For a learning site, the questions might be: “find learner by email,” “show recent lessons,” “check enrolled courses,” and “rank learners by points.” These map naturally to an email lookup hash, list, set, and sorted set rather than one giant serialized profile.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Redis performance engineering combines algorithmic cost, memory behavior, network latency, command selection, and data modeling. Start with hot paths and measure them. Then inspect whether the chosen structure gives the desired operation a reasonable complexity, whether collections are bounded, whether values are unnecessarily large, and whether the client sends commands one at a time. Pipelining and multi-key commands can reduce communication overhead, but they do not fix an inefficient data model. Long-running commands, broad scans, huge sorts, or large responses can affect unrelated requests because server work competes for processing time. Memory pressure can also increase latency and instability, so capacity and headroom belong in performance discussions. The best optimization is often to change the representation so the server can answer the question directly instead of repeatedly computing the answer.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.content: If a dashboard performs 100 individual reads for every page view, first consider whether the access pattern can be consolidated or pipelined. If a request scans a huge collection to find a small subset, redesign the index instead of merely increasing server hardware.

sections.content: Use a loop of measure → identify bottleneck → model the operation → change one variable → benchmark again. Track p95/p99 latency, throughput, memory, command cost, and collection cardinality.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A disciplined Redis debugging workflow starts from the symptom and narrows the scope. If an API is slow, measure client-side latency and identify whether time is spent waiting on Redis, executing commands, or processing results. Slow-log data can reveal expensive server operations, while command monitoring can expose unexpected request patterns during controlled reproduction. If a value is stale, ask whether the read came from a lagging replica, whether a cache entry has an old TTL, or whether a manual index is out of date. If memory is rising, inspect key growth, collection sizes, value sizes, expiration behavior, and replicas. If a multi-step update is inconsistent, examine transaction boundaries, WATCH conflicts, and script logic. The workflow should resist vague conclusions such as “Redis is slow” and instead identify the exact command, key family, workload characteristic, or consistency assumption responsible for the symptom.

The investigation checks whether the application hit `cache:product:55`, whether that key's TTL is longer than intended, whether the source record changed without cache invalidation, and whether a replica was queried before the update had propagated.

topics.title: Common Redis Mistakes
topics.description: Typical modeling, performance, reliability, security, and operational mistakes and how to avoid them.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Common Redis Mistakes is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. The key is to understand what problem the feature solves, what assumptions it makes, and how its cost changes as data and traffic grow. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Common mistakes usually come from treating Redis as either a generic database or a magical cache. Modeling every object as one serialized string can make field updates expensive; creating duplicate full objects can create consistency problems; using global key discovery in request paths can create large blocking operations; and allowing recent-item collections to grow forever can consume memory. Other mistakes include assuming replicas are backups, ignoring replica staleness, sending thousands of commands one by one, writing long Lua scripts, and using TTLs without understanding what happens on a cache miss. Security mistakes include exposing Redis broadly or treating command renaming as sufficient protection. Scaling mistakes include partitioning without understanding key distribution or multi-key access. The common solution is deliberate design: define ownership, access patterns, lifecycle, complexity, consistency, and failure behavior for every important key family.

sections.content: A service stores full customer objects under both customer ID and email, then updates only one copy. It also uses `KEYS` during every request to discover related records. The system now has both correctness and performance problems because the data model is fighting the workload.

sections.content: Review Redis code for duplication, unbounded collections, global scans, sequential round trips, missing TTLs, unclear authority, weak security boundaries, and undefined failure behavior. Fix modeling problems before tuning individual commands.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A useful Redis mental map connects a business question to a structure and then to the command family that operates on it. Whole-value retrieval and counters lead toward strings. This map is more valuable than memorizing isolated commands because it explains why a command belongs in a design. The final choice still depends on version, workload, cardinality, and consistency requirements.

topics.description: A production-oriented checklist for keys, structures, network, complexity, memory, TTL, concurrency, operations, and scaling.

sections.title: Concept
sections.content: Performance Checklist is an important Redis topic because it connects a specific application requirement to a concrete server capability. sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: A production Redis review should cover keys, structures, network behavior, command complexity, memory, expiration, concurrency, operations, and scaling. Keys should be predictable and reasonably compact. Each structure should match its access pattern, and large collections should be bounded where the business permits. Hot paths should avoid unnecessary one-at-a-time round trips and consider batching or pipelining. Every expensive command should be evaluated in terms of N and M and the maximum collection size it can encounter. Memory planning should include replicas and operational headroom. Temporary data should have explicit lifetimes. Multi-step updates should have clear atomicity requirements, and retry loops should be bounded. Operations should have monitoring, slow-log review, backups, replication, and failure procedures. Finally, scaling plans should explain when one instance becomes insufficient and how keys and traffic will be redistributed.

sections.title: Concept

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content: Redis becomes easier to reason about when the major ideas are connected. The core model is key-oriented access plus specialized data structures: strings for scalar or whole-value data, hashes for fields, lists for ordered sequences, sets for unique membership, and sorted sets for scored ordering. Performance depends on complexity, collection size, memory, and network round trips. Explicit indexes and references solve alternate access paths but introduce consistency responsibilities. TTL manages temporary lifecycle, while transactions, WATCH, and focused scripts address coordinated updates. SCAN supports incremental discovery, whereas broad keyspace commands should not become request-path query mechanisms. Replication provides live copies and possible read scaling; backups provide historical recovery. Horizontal scaling distributes data but introduces placement and rebalancing concerns. High availability requires more than a replica: it requires a defined failure and failover path. These principles form a reusable design framework across caches, games, social systems, content platforms, and support applications.

sections.content: When facing a new requirement, ask four questions: What is the most important operation? Which structure represents it directly? How large can that structure become?
